records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name. NC State's page title carries five names (Atlantic Ninebark, Common Ninebark, Eastern Ninebark, Ninebark, Nine Bark), and its Common Name(s) field is a stacked list of those same five entries in the same order as the title, with no entry marked primary; each entry links to its own page under /plants/physocarpus-opulifolius/common-name/ (e.g. .../common-name/common-ninebark/), one per listed name, so none of those pages carries primacy. NC State's own body prose uses the bare name: 'Ninebark is a flowering, deciduous shrub in the rose family and native to central and eastern North America.' MoBot's dedicated species page (kempercode=g840) shows a single field reading 'Common Name: ninebark', with no Common Names popup on this page. RHS's dedicated plant profile instead leads with 'common ninebark' in both its browser-tab title ('Physocarpus opulifolius | common ninebark') and its visible profile subtitle, and has no 'Other common names' section -- its only name-variant block is 'Synonyms', reading 'Spiraea opulifolia'. common_name is Ninebark because that is what MoBot's dedicated species page gives in its single Common Name field and what NC State's own prose calls the plant; 'Common Ninebark' is the RHS variant.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: Clemson's HGIC factsheet (a dedicated single-species rain-garden page titled 'Rain Garden Plants:(Physocarpus opulifolius)') mentions that excessive doses of bark decoctions historically used by Native Americans can be toxic, but this is a human/historical-use mention, not scoped to cats or dogs, so per the schema rules it cannot support toxic_to_pets=true. NC State's Plant Type and Problems tag lists carry no 'Poisonous' or 'Poisonous to Humans' tag for this species (no Poison block exists on that page), and RHS's page has no Toxicity section. This Clemson quote could not be independently re-verified against the live page (the page is behind a Cloudflare bot challenge that blocked a direct fetch), so it was excluded from the citations array entirely rather than risk an unverifiable quote.

water_regime left null: the only structured moisture field found is MoBot's 'Water: Dry to medium,' which is mid-scale and, per the schema rules, cannot support keep_moist; NC State's Culture prose repeats the same 'dry to medium' language. Neither phrasing maps cleanly onto any of the four water_regime enum values, and no admissible source frames this in-ground shrub's watering as a moist/dry cycling instruction, so the field is left null with MoBot's 'Dry to medium' noted here as a disclosed mid-scale counterpoint.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null even though NC State's Soil pH field includes a closed 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band: RHS's own pH field independently lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' as all acceptable, and NC State's Soil pH field itself also separately lists open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' and 'Alkaline (>8.0)' bands alongside Neutral -- so no ceiling or floor is supportable in either direction, per the schema rule that RHS acceptance of alkaline soils nulls the max and acceptance of acid soils nulls the min.

records.name_note: All three sources point the same direction but differ on which single name they foreground. NC State's Common Name(s) field for Rhus aromatica lists six entries in alphabetical order -- 'Aromatic Sumac', 'Fragrant Sumac', 'Lemon Sumac', 'Polecat Bush', 'Polecat Sumac', 'Sumac' -- and marks no primary; its first entry, 'Aromatic Sumac', is the alphabetically first name and also the first name in the page title's parenthetical, so it carries no primacy of its own. NC State's separate page for the sibling species Rhus trilobata carries both 'Aromatic Sumac' and 'Fragrant Sumac' among its own alphabetized common names, so on NC State neither name is unique to this species. The two sources that do state a lead both converge on fragrant sumac: Missouri Botanical Garden's page renders 'Common Name: fragrant sumac' as a single value (a three-name Common Names list -- fragrant sumac, lemon sumac, polecat bush -- exists only inside an overlib tooltip attribute in the link's markup, so it is not quoted here), and RHS's plant-profile subtitle for the species page (not the 'Gro-low' cultivar page) reads 'fragrant sumach', with an Other common names field reading 'fragrant sumach, lemon sumac, polecat bush' and a Synonyms field reading 'Rhus canadensis'. 'Fragrant Sumac' is chosen because it is the name led by both sources that state a lead.
records.toxicity_detail: Missouri Botanical Garden's Noteworthy Characteristics section states that although the leaves of Rhus aromatica resemble those of the related poison ivy (Rhus radicans, i.e. Toxicodendron radicans) in appearance, "fragrant sumac is a totally non-poisonous plant." This statement is general/unscoped — it does not name cats or dogs specifically, and no admissible source addresses pet toxicity for this species, so toxic_to_pets is left null (see unknowns) even though this is direct evidence the plant carries no known poison hazard to humans generally. No admissible source (including NC State, which has no Poison block/Poisonous tag for this species) documents a toxic principle, symptoms, or a toxic plant part for Rhus aromatica.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity evidence found (MoBot's 'totally non-poisonous plant' statement, contrasting the species with poison ivy) is unscoped to any animal, human or pet -- it does not name cats or dogs, so per the scoping rule it cannot support a true OR false determination for toxic_to_pets specifically.

No admissible source carries a structured 'is often confused with:' module for Rhus aromatica (checked NC State's main species page and its common-name alias pages). The poison-ivy resemblance is instead documented only as prose in MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics section, quoted in toxicity_detail.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field for this species is the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band, which per the schema rule cannot be used to set a floor or ceiling. RHS's pH field could not be confirmed on the rendered species page (WebFetch of the RHS profile did not surface a rendered Soil/pH field for this species), so no cross-check value from RHS is available either.

water_regime left null: the only structured moisture fields found are mid/low-scale descriptors -- NC State's soil-drainage tags ('Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry') and MoBot's structured field 'Water: Dry to medium' plus its Culture prose 'dry to medium, well-drained soil' -- none of which is a literal watering-cadence statement matching the keep_moist/keep_barely_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between enum built for container/houseplant watering. Disclosed here rather than force-mapped.

day/night temperature fields, humidity fields, light footcandle fields, water day-interval fields, and fertilizer fields are all null because Rhus aromatica is an in-ground hardy landscape shrub (USDA zones 3-9 per NC State) and no admissible source frames its care in those terms -- consistent with the rule to leave such fields null for in-ground shrubs absent source framing.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's only 'full sun' hour figure found ('6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day') is the site-wide light-category legend text, not species-specific prose, so per the schema rule it is excluded.

Clemson HGIC, Penn State Extension, UMD Extension, UF/IFAS (edis/ask.ifas), and UGA fieldreport.caes.uga.edu were searched but returned no dedicated Rhus aromatica publication -- only passing mentions of sumacs generically or of other Rhus species -- so none of these five admissible domains contributed a usable species-specific claim for this record.

RHS's Size, Time to Maturity, Hardiness, Soil type, Moisture, pH, Position/Sun exposure, Aspect and Exposure fields render as empty headers with no values on this species page, so none was used; only the Common Name subtitle, Other common names, Synonyms, Family, Native to GB/Ireland, Genus description, Name Status and Plant Range render as extractable text. Note that unauthenticated direct fetches of this URL intermittently return a cached page for an entirely different species (Corylus americana was returned on one attempt), so RHS content for this record must be confirmed against a response whose title reads 'Rhus aromatica | fragrant sumach' before use.
